## Simple explanation

An activation function transforms a neuron's input into its output. It lets a
neural network represent more than simple linear relationships.

## Technical explanation

A neuron first combines its inputs, usually as a weighted sum plus a bias,
then applies an activation function. Common choices include ReLU, sigmoid,
tanh, and GELU. The choice affects the network's output range, gradient
behaviour, and computational properties.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Activation functions are part of a model's architecture. Their behaviour
affects training stability, gradient flow, and suitability for a task, while
the final layer's activation can determine how predictions are represented.

## How it works

For a pre-activation value \(z = w^\top x + b\), the neuron outputs
\(a = f(z)\). For example, ReLU is \(f(z) = \max(0,z)\), while sigmoid maps
real values to the interval \((0,1)\). A sigmoid output can represent a
binary probability when used with an appropriate loss and training setup.

## Practical example

A hidden layer might apply ReLU to each weighted sum. Negative values become
zero and positive values pass through, adding non-linearity before the next
layer.

## Common misconceptions

- A neural network can be reduced to a linear model if all its layers are
  linear, regardless of how many such layers it contains.
- No single activation function is best for every layer and task.
- A sigmoid output is not automatically a calibrated probability.
